description_full: PVH Corp., together with its subsidiaries, operates as an apparel company in the United States and internationally. The company operates through Tommy Hilfiger North America, Tommy Hilfiger International, Calvin Klein North America, Calvin Klein International, and Heritage Brands Wholesale segments. It designs and markets men's, women's, and children's branded apparel, footwear and accessories, underwear, home furnishings, luggage, dresses, suits and swimwear, activewear, sportswear, socks and accessories, outerwear, golf products, watches and jewelry, eyeglasses and non-ophthalmic sunglasses, jeans wear, performance apparel, intimate apparel, dress shirts, handbags, fragrance, small leather goods, and other related products. The company offers its products under its own brands, such as TOMMY HILFIGER, TOMMY JEANS, Calvin Klein, Calvin Klein Jeans, Calvin Klein Underwear, Calvin Klein collection, and Calvin Klein sport, as well as various other owned, licensed, and private label brands. It distributes its products at wholesale in department, chain, and specialty stores; through warehouse clubs, mass market, and off-price and independent retailers; and through company-operated full-price, outlet stores, and concession locations; and through digital commerce sites. PVH Corp. was formerly known as Phillips-Van Heusen Corporation and changed its name to PVH Corp. in June 2011. The company was founded in 1881 and is based in New York, New York.

financial_summary: PVH Corp. is a mid-cap consumer cyclical business with a $4.2B market cap on $9.0B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -0% over the past three years and +1% annually across the full decade — essentially flat, and a business treading water is rarely a path to compounding.
Returns on capital run at 10% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically. Gross margins of 54% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $538M in free cash flow — roughly 6 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 26.89× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.2× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and thin 2.4× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 14.1% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.3× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 3% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Cyclical median (8%).
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.32x its revenue share).
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.1% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 380 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 19% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 11% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 48% and a beta of 1.23, it amplifies market moves.
About $66.1M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 73% in the 2020 crash, 60% in the 2022 bear market and 71% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 47% below its DCF fair value of $169, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 58%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $118 to $246 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 7.2 vs 17.7, EV/EBITDA 8.2 vs 10.5 and P/FCF 7.7 vs 15.8 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 199% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 12.9% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The 11 covering analysts target $92.82 on average, 3% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 10% earns above the cost of capital of 8.6%, but the 1pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.99).
It runs a 54% gross margin and converts 6% of revenue into free cash flow.
ROE of 1% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.4x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.5% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 3.2x net debt to EBITDA ($701.5M of cash against $2.3B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 2.4x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -0.3% over 3 years, 4.6% over 5 years and 1.1% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 15%).
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 10.0% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 2.7% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.5x depreciation (1.6% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 10, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.1%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insider trading is two-way: 1 purchase and 3 sales over the past year, net $358K bought.
It returns 14.1% a year to shareholders (13.9% in buybacks and 0.2% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 8.0% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
Short interest is elevated at 11.8% of the float, 4.8 days to cover.
people: With about 15,000 employees, each generates about $597K of revenue, 1.6x the Consumer Cyclical median, and revenue has grown 4.5% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $36K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.9M (7x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
